name: Cerebral cortex (context envelope)
function: The folded gray matter of the cerebral hemispheres supports perception, action, language, cognition and memory in interacting networks. Most is six-layered neocortex; hippocampal and olfactory allocortex have different lamination. Cortical thickness and areal boundaries vary across regions and individuals.
contextNote: The hemisphere ribbon is derived by dilation/subtraction of a cerebral white-matter surface, not a measured cortical gray-matter segmentation. It has no independently registered sulci, gyri, cortical thickness or functional parcels. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.

afferent: Thalamocortical relays and reciprocal association/commissural connections
Basal-forebrain cholinergic and brainstem monoaminergic modulation
efferent: Corticofugal projections to thalamus, striatum, brainstem and spinal cord, depending on cortical area
Association and callosal projections to other cortical regions

bloodSupply: ACA supplies much of medial frontal/anterior parietal cortex, MCA most lateral convexity and insula, and PCA medial occipital/inferomedial temporal cortex. Borders and collateral flow vary.

clinical.findings: Deficits depend on region and network involvement; aphasia, neglect, field loss, seizures or discriminative sensory deficits may occur.
ACA-MCA or MCA-PCA border-zone injury can follow impaired perfusion; symptoms vary with location and extent.

name: Frontal lobe
function: The frontal lobe lies anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Motor/premotor regions support action and gaze, while prefrontal and cingulate networks contribute to executive control, motivation, social judgment and language in the dominant hemisphere.

afferent: VA/VL motor and MD association thalamic relays
Parietal/temporal association and basal-ganglia/cerebellar loops
efferent: Corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine projections from appropriate motor regions
Corticostriatal, corticothalamic and association/commissural projections

bloodSupply: MCA supplies most lateral frontal cortex; ACA supplies much of the medial frontal surface and a superior strip. Territories vary.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness and dominant-hemisphere nonfluent aphasia; leg involvement varies with lesion extent.
May cause reduced initiation or abulia; involvement of paracentral/SMA regions can add leg-predominant weakness or reduced speech.
Executive, motivational or behavioral changes depend on lesion site and interacting networks; no single frontal-lobe syndrome is obligatory.

name: Parietal lobe
function: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, above the lateral temporal region and anterior to the occipital boundary. Postcentral cortex processes somatic input, while superior/inferior parietal and medial parietal networks contribute to body representation, attention, praxis and language-related functions.

afferent: VPL/VPM somatosensory thalamocortical input to postcentral cortex
Visual, auditory, frontal and association thalamic inputs to parietal networks
efferent: Reciprocal frontal/temporal/occipital and callosal connections
Corticofugal projections, including a contribution to corticospinal pathways

bloodSupply: MCA supplies most lateral parietal cortex; ACA supplies anterior medial parietal/paracentral cortex and PCA more posterior medial areas. The precuneus may span ACA/PCA territories.

clinical.findings: Right-predominant attention-network injury can produce left neglect; dominant parietal injury can impair praxis, calculation, writing or language, depending on extent.
Can impair contralateral discriminative touch, proprioception and cortical sensory tasks; crude sensation is not invariably preserved.
clinical.vascular: MCA lateral or ACA medial sensorimotor branches

clinical.findings: Acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation may occur with dominant parietal network injury; an isolated angular-gyrus lesion is not the only explanation.

name: Temporal lobe
function: The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus. Superior temporal cortex participates in hearing and language networks, ventral occipitotemporal cortex in object/face recognition, and medial temporal structures in memory and emotion. Temporal optic-radiation fibres, including Meyer's loop, convey contralateral superior visual-field information.

afferent: MGN auditory radiation to primary auditory cortex
Association-cortical inputs to temporal visual, language and medial temporal networks
efferent: Association pathways to frontal/parietal/occipital regions
Hippocampal outputs through fornix/entorhinal routes and amygdalar outputs to cortical/subcortical targets

bloodSupply: MCA supplies most lateral temporal cortex; PCA supplies much inferomedial temporal cortex/hippocampal formation. Anterior choroidal contributions to anterior medial structures are variable.

clinical.findings: May cause fluent aphasia; injury to temporal optic radiations may add contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
Memory impairment depends on laterality, bilaterality and network extent; a visual field defect requires involvement of visual pathways.
clinical.vascular: PCA/anterior choroidal territories or nonvascular causes

clinical.findings: May produce experiential or autonomic auras, automatisms and impaired awareness; these features are not specific to one nucleus.

name: Occipital lobe
function: The occipital lobe contains primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus and multiple extrastriate areas. V1 maps the contralateral visual hemifield; interconnected visual association regions process form, color, motion and spatial relationships.

afferent: LGN via optic radiation to V1
Reciprocal extrastriate, pulvinar and callosal connections
efferent: Interconnected dorsal parietal and ventral temporal visual networks
Corticothalamic and other descending visual projections

bloodSupply: Mainly PCA calcarine/parieto-occipital branches, with variable MCA contributions to lateral/polar cortex and collateral flow.

clinical.findings: Unilateral visual-cortex injury may cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia or a smaller homonymous defect; macular sparing is possible, not obligatory.
May cause cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light responses. Some patients have denial/confabulation (Anton syndrome), but this is not universal.
A classic pattern follows dominant (usually left) occipital plus splenial injury, disconnecting visual input from language networks.

name: Insula
function: The insula is buried in the lateral sulcus and covered by frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. Its long/short gyri and anterior-posterior cytoarchitectural gradient participate in taste, somatic/visceral sensation, salience, emotion and autonomic regulation within wider networks.

afferent: Thalamic somatosensory/gustatory and association inputs
Reciprocal anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal, temporal and amygdalar connections
efferent: Cortical salience/interoceptive networks
Connections with hypothalamic and brainstem autonomic systems

bloodSupply: MCA insular (M2) branches. Deep lenticulostriate branches usually arise from proximal MCA and supply different deep territories; insular and basal-ganglia supply should not be equated.

clinical.findings: May affect taste, somatic/visceral awareness, speech or autonomic regulation. Isolated deficits and laterality effects are variable.
Can include throat discomfort, somatic sensations or autonomic symptoms; clinical semiology alone does not prove insular onset.

name: Limbic lobe
function: The traditional limbic lobe is a morphological grouping of medial cortical regions including cingulate and parahippocampal cortex. These areas participate in distributed memory, motivational and affective networks; the term does not define a single isolated emotion system.

afferent: Association cortex and anterior/MD thalamic inputs, varying by subregion
Amygdalar and hippocampal/parahippocampal network connections
efferent: Cingulum and other association connections between medial cortical regions
Hippocampal output via fornix and cortical routes; cortical/subcortical motivational connections

bloodSupply: ACA supplies much anterior cingulate/subcallosal cortex; PCA contributes posterior cingulate/retrosplenial and inferomedial temporal supply. Anterior medial temporal supply varies.

clinical.findings: Can cause subacute memory disturbance, seizures and behavioral changes, often with medial temporal involvement; MRI findings and antibody associations vary.
Posterior medial or medial temporal lesions may impair memory or orientation depending on extent.

name: Cingulate gyrus
function: The cingulate gyrus arches above the corpus callosum and continues posteriorly toward the parahippocampal region. Anterior/midcingulate regions contribute to motivation, control, pain affect and action; posterior cingulate/retrosplenial regions participate in memory and spatial/contextual processing.

afferent: Anterior and association thalamic inputs
Frontal, parietal, medial temporal, insular and amygdalar connections
efferent: Cingulum/association projections to frontal, medial parietal and parahippocampal regions
Subcortical motivational, motor and autonomic network projections, varying by subregion

bloodSupply: ACA branches supply much anterior/midcingulate cortex; PCA supplies posterior cingulate/retrosplenial regions, with variable overlap.

clinical.findings: Can contribute to abulia; extensive bilateral damage may produce akinetic mutism. Limb weakness requires involvement of motor pathways.
May impair episodic memory or topographical orientation.

name: Parahippocampal gyrus
function: This medial temporal gyrus lies medial to the collateral/rhinal sulcus and is continuous with the cingulate isthmus posteriorly. Its anterior entorhinal/perirhinal regions and posterior parahippocampal cortex link association cortex with hippocampal memory networks; the boundaries of these cortical areas do not coincide with the whole gyrus.

afferent: Perirhinal and multimodal association-cortical inputs
Posterior cingulate/retrosplenial, entorhinal and amygdalar connections
efferent: Entorhinal pathways to hippocampal formation and reciprocal cortical return
Cingulum/association connections to medial and lateral association cortex

bloodSupply: Mainly PCA temporal branches, with variable anterior choroidal and other anterior contributions.

clinical.findings: May impair memory or scene/context recognition; associated field loss requires visual-pathway involvement.
Medial temporal injury can cause memory impairment and seizures; infection and autoimmunity are among the possible causes.

name: Planum temporale
synonyms: auditory association cortex of the superior temporal plane (host gyrus of A2)
function: The planum temporale is the superior temporal surface posterior to Heschl's gyri. It participates in auditory association and auditory-motor/language networks. Population-level asymmetry does not establish an individual's language dominance or diagnose dyslexia.

afferent: Primary and surrounding auditory cortex
Temporal/parietal association and interhemispheric connections
efferent: Reciprocal superior temporal/inferior parietal and frontal auditory-language networks
Descending corticothalamic auditory modulation

bloodSupply: Predominantly MCA temporal/insular branches; arterial patterns vary.

clinical.findings: Can impair recognition or analysis of speech or other sounds; bilateral and dominant-hemisphere lesions may produce different patterns.
Aphasia depends on dominant temporal/parietal network involvement; the planum temporale is not identical to Wernicke's area.

name: Precentral gyrus
function: The frontal gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus and posterior to the precentral sulcus. It contains much of M1, including cortex on the anterior bank of the central sulcus; motor-area boundaries do not follow the whole gyrus exactly.

afferent: Motor thalamic and sensorimotor/premotor inputs
efferent: Corticospinal/corticobulbar and other motor-network outputs

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA lateral branches; medial continuation approaches ACA paracentral territory.

clinical.findings: Can impair contralateral voluntary movement, with distribution depending on the injured cortical/subcortical territory.

name: Postcentral gyrus
function: The parietal gyrus immediately posterior to the central sulcus and anterior to the postcentral sulcus. S1 areas occupy its crown/banks and medial continuation, with different cytoarchitectural and somatic representations.

afferent: VPL/VPM thalamocortical and somatosensory-network inputs
efferent: S2, posterior parietal and motor-network projections; corticothalamic return

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA lateral branches; medial paracentral continuation mainly ACA.

clinical.findings: May impair contralateral sensory discrimination/proprioception and cortical sensory tasks; interpretation depends on primary sensation and cognition.

name: Paracentral lobule
function: The medial cortical region around the continuation of the precentral/postcentral gyri, bounded by the paracentral and marginal cingulate sulci. Its anterior and posterior parts contain lower-limb motor and somatosensory representations respectively.

afferent: Motor/somatosensory thalamic and cortical inputs
efferent: Motor descending and sensory-association projections, varying by anterior/posterior part

bloodSupply: Predominantly ACA paracentral/pericallosal/callosomarginal branches.

clinical.findings: Often causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness or sensory change. Incontinence/abulia may accompany wider medial frontal injury; they are not intrinsic to every lobular lesion.

name: Superior frontal gyrus
function: The superior frontal gyrus lies above the superior frontal sulcus and continues onto the medial frontal surface. It spans several motor-association and prefrontal territories, so it should not be assigned one function.

afferent: Frontal/parietal association and motor/association thalamic inputs
efferent: Reciprocal cortical and basal-ganglia/thalamic networks; motor outputs in appropriate posterior portions

bloodSupply: ACA medially and MCA laterally, with border-zone variation.

clinical.findings: Executive, initiation or motor deficits depend on which posterior/medial/prefrontal portions and connections are involved.

name: Middle frontal gyrus
function: The middle frontal gyrus lies between superior and inferior frontal sulci. It includes portions of lateral prefrontal cortex and posterior frontal eye-field/premotor networks; neither a single Brodmann area nor a single functional system defines the whole gyrus.

afferent: Association-cortical and thalamic inputs
efferent: Frontoparietal, corticostriatal and thalamocortical networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly MCA frontal branches; superior border varies.

clinical.findings: Can affect executive control, attention or eye movements according to network and location.

name: Inferior frontal gyrus
synonyms: pars opercularis (part of inferior frontal gyrus)
pars triangularis (part of inferior frontal gyrus)
pars orbitalis (part of inferior frontal gyrus)
function: This frontal gyrus below the inferior frontal sulcus has opercular, triangular and orbital portions defined by rami of the lateral sulcus. Dominant opercular/triangular cortex overlaps the conventional Broca region, while both hemispheres participate in broader language, control and social/affective networks.

afferent: Temporal/parietal and other frontal association inputs
efferent: Reciprocal language/control networks and premotor/striatal projections

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA frontal/opercular branches, with anterior/orbital variation.

clinical.findings: May cause aphasia or motor-speech/control deficits; language dominance and lesion extent matter.

name: Superior parietal lobule
function: The lateral parietal region above the intraparietal sulcus and behind postcentral gyrus. It integrates somatosensory and visual information for body representation, spatial analysis and visually guided actions within parietofrontal networks.

afferent: Somatosensory, visual association and thalamic inputs
efferent: Premotor/frontal and parietal association networks

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA parietal branches, with variable ACA/PCA border contributions.

clinical.findings: Can impair body/spatial integration or visually guided reaching. Bilateral parieto-occipital network injury can contribute to Balint syndrome; this is not a one-lobule diagnostic rule.

name: Angular gyrus
function: The posterior inferior parietal gyrus around the end of the superior temporal sulcus, posterior to the supramarginal gyrus. It participates in distributed language, calculation, semantic, attention and multimodal networks; functional subdivisions and laterality vary.

afferent: Temporal, visual and parietal association inputs
efferent: Frontal/temporal and medial association networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly MCA angular/inferior-division branches, with MCA/PCA border variation.

clinical.findings: May impair reading, writing, calculation or praxis; Gerstmann features can occur, but are not obligatory or confined to angular cortex.
Right-predominant parietal network damage may contribute to left neglect; the network includes other cortical/subcortical sites.

name: Supramarginal gyrus
function: The anterior inferior parietal gyrus wrapping around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus. It contributes to somatosensory integration, praxis, phonological/auditory-motor processing and attention in interacting parietofrontal/temporal networks.

afferent: Somatosensory, temporal auditory-language and association inputs
efferent: Frontal/premotor and temporal/parietal connections

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA parietal/inferior-division branches, with variation.

clinical.findings: Can contribute to apraxia, repetition/phonological impairment or attention deficits depending on hemisphere and network extent.

name: Precuneus
function: The medial parietal cortex anterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus and behind the marginal branch of the cingulate sulcus, above posterior cingulate cortex. It participates in visuospatial imagery, self-related processing and episodic/contextual networks; it is distinct from cuneus and retrosplenial cortex.

afferent: Medial/lateral parietal, visual and memory/association-network inputs
efferent: Reciprocal parietal, frontal and medial temporal association connections

bloodSupply: Variable ACA and PCA medial parietal contributions.

clinical.findings: May impair spatial orientation, integration or memory-related tasks; no single unique symptom establishes precuneus injury.

name: Superior temporal gyrus
synonyms: Heschl transverse gyri on superior plane
function: The superior lateral temporal gyrus lies below the lateral sulcus and above the superior temporal sulcus. Its superior plane contains auditory core/association regions; posterior dominant temporal portions participate in language networks, while sulcal and gyral subdivisions support broader auditory/social processing.

afferent: Auditory thalamic/cortical and multimodal association inputs
efferent: Temporal, parietal and frontal association networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly MCA temporal/insular branches.

clinical.findings: Can alter auditory processing or dominant language comprehension; bilateral central auditory injury can cause more severe hearing-recognition deficits.

name: Middle temporal gyrus
function: The lateral temporal gyrus between superior and middle temporal sulci. It participates in distributed semantic, multimodal and visual/language association networks; a gyral label does not define one cytoarchitectural field.

afferent: Temporal/occipital and other association-cortical inputs
efferent: Frontal/parietal and temporal association networks

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA temporal branches, with posterior border variation.

clinical.findings: May affect semantic, language or visual association functions depending on side and extent.

name: Inferior temporal gyrus
function: The inferior lateral/basal temporal gyrus below the middle temporal sulcus and lateral to the inferior temporal sulcus. It contributes to visual-object and semantic processing within ventral occipitotemporal networks.

afferent: Ventral occipital/temporal visual-association inputs
efferent: Anterior temporal and frontal association networks; reciprocal ventral-stream projections

bloodSupply: Variable MCA lateral and PCA inferior temporal contributions.

clinical.findings: May impair object/semantic recognition; clinical expression depends on distributed network damage and laterality.

name: Fusiform (occipitotemporal) gyrus
function: The basal occipitotemporal gyrus lies between inferior temporal sulcus laterally and collateral sulcus medially. Parts support face, object, color and visual-word processing in ventral visual networks; the whole gyrus is not one face area or one word-form area.

afferent: Ventral occipital/temporal visual and multimodal association inputs
efferent: Reciprocal temporal semantic/recognition and frontal language-related networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly PCA inferior temporal/occipital branches with anterior/lateral MCA overlap.

clinical.findings: Face-recognition impairment often follows right or bilateral ventral occipitotemporal network injury; it is not obligatory after every fusiform lesion.
Dominant ventral occipitotemporal and connecting-pathway injury can impair reading; this differs from a single universal word-form coordinate.

name: Cuneus
function: The wedge-shaped medial occipital cortex between the parieto-occipital sulcus and calcarine sulcus. V1 on the upper calcarine bank represents the contralateral lower visual field; other cuneal portions include extrastriate cortex.

afferent: LGN input to V1 and visual association inputs
efferent: Interconnected visual cortical and thalamic networks

bloodSupply: Mainly PCA calcarine/parieto-occipital branches.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral inferior visual-field loss; size and retinotopic extent determine the pattern.

name: Lingual gyrus
function: The medial basal occipital gyrus below the calcarine sulcus and above the collateral sulcus. Lower-bank V1 represents the contralateral upper visual field; adjoining cortex contributes to ventral visual processing.

afferent: LGN input to V1 and visual association connections
efferent: Interconnected ventral visual and thalamic networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly PCA calcarine/temporal-occipital branches.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral superior visual-field loss; associated visual-recognition changes require involvement of corresponding networks.

name: Retrosplenial cortex
function: The small medial cortical region around/behind the splenium, adjacent to posterior cingulate and the cingulate isthmus. It participates in contextual memory and spatial orientation through medial temporal, thalamic and medial parietal connections. Retrosplenial cortex is not identical to the whole posterior cingulate or precuneus.

afferent: Anterior thalamic and hippocampal/parahippocampal/medial cortical inputs
efferent: Reciprocal medial temporal, cingulate and parietal association networks

bloodSupply: Predominantly PCA splenial/posterior medial branches, with variation.

clinical.findings: May cause topographical disorientation or memory difficulties; lesion extent and connecting white matter influence the presentation.
